title: Adaptive tenant headroom and penalty box playbook
content:
Purpose / quick summary:
This note captures a proposal for an adaptive tenant-level headroom model + penalty-box mechanism to reduce noisy-neighbor incidents across regions while preserving SLA guarantees for contracted tenants. The goal is a pragmatic, observable control-plane behavior that: 1) predicts imminent contention per-tenant, 2) applies graduated mitigations (soft shaping -> burst reservoir -> penalty box -> eviction) and 3) coordinates global policy from a regional-aware controller to respect data residency and regional SLAs.

Why we need this (problem statement):
- Increasing multi-tenant pressure: we see more tenants with spiky token/sec patterns and large variance in seq lengths. Static quotas / token budgets alone are either too loose (noisy neighbors) or too conservative (wastes headroom for healthy tenants).
- Multi-region complexity: tenants may route to different regions based on latency/cost. A noisy tenant in a single region can starve regional pools and trigger fallbacks for other tenants in that region even if global capacity exists elsewhere.
- SLA obligations: some tenants have contract SLAs for p95 latency and minimum throughput, which must take precedence over best-effort accounts.
- Observability gaps: current alarms are host/instance-centric; we need tenant-centric signals at the control plane to act early.

Objectives (measurable):
- Reduce tenant-caused P95 violations by 60% for impacted regions in 90 days after rollout.
- Limit automated full-evictions to <1/month across platform during steady-state.
- Detect and apply soft shaping within 30s of a predicted capacity violation.

Core concepts / glossary (brief):
- Headroom: estimated spare serving capacity for a tenant in a region over the next T seconds (default T=120s). Expressed in tokens/sec or concurrent requests.
- Burst reservoir: temporary allowance above baseline quota funded from pooled capacity for short spikes (default duration 30s).
- Penalty box: a rate-limited state for a tenant in a region after repeated/massive violations; requests are delayed or redirected to lower-cost/compatibility models with visible error codes.
- Regional soft-fence: a per-tenant soft quota enforced by routing agents inside a region that attempts degradation rather than hard drop.
- Probation window: time after a penalty where the tenant is allowed limited traffic back to re-evaluate behavior.

Signals we will monitor and use for decisioning:
- Tenant request rate (rps / tokens/sec) per region
- Token distribution by sequence-length buckets (short/medium/long)
- GPU queue length and real-time token processing rate per serving group
- P95 and P99 latency per tenant + route
- Error and model-fallback counts (per tenant)
- Pending requests and queue age (tail age metric)
- Recent rollback/rollout health indicators (if a tenant’s model changed)
- Billing/contract tier mapping (priority)

Predictive headroom model (sketch):
1) Input: time-series for rps (5s bins), tokens/sec, sequence-length mix, recent P95 latency, GPU utilization for the region.
2) Forecast: simple exponentially-weighted moving average + short-horizon linear extrapolation (T=120s). We intentionally avoid heavy ML for first iteration to keep behavior explainable.
3) Headroom calc: region_capacity_for_group - forecasted_total_demand + tenant_expected_release_rate. Attach confidence interval (low/medium/high) based on variance.
4) Outputs: predicted deficit (tokens/sec) and recommended mitigation level: none, soft_shape, use_burst, penalty_box_probation.

Routing / Control-plane architecture (how decisions are enforced):
- Global controller (read-only for per-region telemetry + write for tenant-level policy bindings): maintains global tenant priority map, contract SLAs, and cross-region fallback rules. Runs in private control plane and is HA.
- Regional agents (enforcement plane): subscribe to local telemetry, compute headroom per tenant with the forecast model, and enforce soft-fence, burst reservoir, and penalty box locally. Agents also report back to the global controller every 10s with action summaries.
- Fallback router: a fast-path layer that can redirect requests to fallback regions or fallback model variants when local enforcement would cause SLA breaches.

Enforcement states and transitions (state machine):
- NORMAL: tenant under quota, no mitigations.
- SOFT_SHAPED: token rate reduced by up to X% (configurable by tier), no hard rejects. Applied when predicted headroom low but confidence medium.
- BURSTING: tenant permitted short bursts from pooled reservoir. Bounded by reservoir budget and cooldown.
- PENALTY_BOX: tenant traffic rate-limited and optionally routed to degraded model. Applied after N violations in M minutes or a predicted sustained deficit high-confidence.
- EVICTED: rare, last-resort: tenant requests rejected locally and must use alternate region or wait for administrative action.

Transition examples:
- NORMAL -> SOFT_SHAPED: predicted deficit > threshold_small AND confidence >= medium -> apply rate limit of min(soft_limit_by_tier, X%).
- SOFT_SHAPED -> BURSTING: tenant still exceeds soft_ceil but reservoir available -> allow short bursts and start reservoir decrement timer.
- SOFT_SHAPED -> PENALTY_BOX: repeated over-limit events (N=3) inside probation window or latency P99 > SLA multiplier -> escalate.
- PENALTY_BOX -> PROBATION (a lightweight NORMAL): after cooldown (default 10m) allow small fraction back and re-evaluate.

Policy mapping to customer tiers / contracts:
- Tier: enterprise (contracted SLA): smallest soft shaping, large dedicated reservoir share, penalty box only after extreme violations or manual approvals. Automatic regional failover prioritized for enterprise.
- Tier: standard: moderate soft shaping, smaller burst allotment, default penalty box cooldowns.
- Tier: free / community: aggressive soft shaping, limited/no burst, shorter probation before penalty box.

Noisy-neighbor controls (practical mitigations):
- Prefix caching and KV reuse prioritization: ensure expensive repeated prefixes belonging to high-tier customers are cached and pinned where possible.
- Per-tenant micro-batching knobs: limit batch size for tenants causing long tail latencies.
- Model-variant degrade: automatic fallback to smaller/quantized variants when penalized (explicitly listed in tenant binding).
- Graceful request diversion: for non-critical tenants, respond with 429 + structured payload that indicates reason and expected retry window; include headers for clients to adapt.

Observability and debugging surfaced to SRE / SE teams:
- Tenant timeline: a single-pane view showing headroom forecast, state transitions, reservoir usage, and region-level capacity curves.
- Timeline drilldowns to offending request IDs and sequence length distribution at the time of event.
- Audit log entries for all control-plane actions with justification (predicted_deficit, confidence).
- Synthetic probes: per-tenant synthetic load tests run daily in a canary region to validate headroom calibration.

Operational playbook (runbook snippets):
- If a regional P95 spike observed with multiple tenants -> check regional agent summary; identify tenants in PENALTY_BOX or high reservoir usage.
- To relieve pressure temporarily: increase region burst reservoir from global pool (requires manual override via controller UI + audit log). Use only for enterprise incidents.
- If a tenant repeatedly hits PENALTY_BOX across regions -> contact SE for review, may require contract change, dedicated capacity offer, or model/traffic changes.

Safety and fairness knobs:
- Fairshare decay: reservoir credits decay over a sliding window to prevent perpetual advantage by bursty tenants.
- Probation multiplier: make escalation slower if tenant has good historical behavior (historical score).
- Manual override exceptions: support staff with the right role can escalate or pin a tenant to NORMAL for a limited window; all overrides are audited.

Experiments / rollout plan (v1 -> v3):
- v1 (controlled): deploy regional agents in 2 pilot regions with conservative thresholds; only observe and suggest actions (dry-run) for 2 weeks. Compare predicted deficits vs actual.
- v2 (soft enforcement): enable SOFT_SHAPED and BURSTING enforcement in pilots. Ramp telemetry dashboards and add synthetic probes. Run for 4 weeks, iterate thresholds.
- v3 (global enforcement + penalty box): enable PENALTY_BOX with human-in-the-loop alerting for enterprise tenants only. Expand to all regions if stability targets met.

Open questions / design decisions to resolve:
- Default T for forecast horizon: 60s vs 120s? Short horizon reduces false positives but increases reactivity.
- Reservoir sizing approach: static fraction of region capacity vs dynamic allocation driven by weekly usage patterns.
- Penalty box UX: return degraded model vs 429 — which leads to better downstream behavior for client apps?
- Cross-region fairness: should global headroom be abstracted or always region-local? (tradeoffs: cross-region fairness vs data residency/latency).

Next steps / action items (owners):
- (Maya) implement minimal forecast prototype inside regional agent (PR: GH: platform#1482). Due 2025-02-25.
- (Arjun) build tenant timeline dashboard wireframe and link into observability. Due 2025-03-04.
- (Sofie) draft penalty-box client API contract and error codes spec. Due 2025-02-28.
- (Liam) run historical backtest of forecast +/- threshold parameters on last 6 months of telemetry. Due 2025-03-07.

Appendix: example policy snippets (pseudo-config)
- tenant_policy: {
    tenant_id: "acct-3112",
    tier: "standard",
    soft_shape_pct: 20,
    burst_allowance: 12000_tokens_per_minute,
    penalty_box_thresholds: { over_limit_count: 3, window_minutes: 5, p99_multiplier: 3 }
  }

- reservoir_config: {
    region: "us-west-2",
    pool_size_tokens_per_minute: 300000,
    per_tenant_max_pct: 20
  }

(we will publish actual JSON schema for policies when we finalize config names; above is intentionally human-readable).

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus review on transition thresholds, telemetry signals, and the enterprise exception flow. If we want earlier enforcement for free-tier customers, we should mark that explicitly and schedule a communication plan.
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: start with explainable forecast + conservative enforcement, iterate toward more aggressive automatic mitigations as confidence grows.

End of note.
